name: hook
text: How does a calculator find the cosine of a number when all it can really do is add and multiply? It fakes the curve with a polynomial.

name: setup
text: Start with cosine of x near zero. At x equals zero, the height is one, so our simplest flat guess is just P of x equals one.

name: slope
text: Next, match the slope. Cosine's derivative at zero is zero, so the tangent line stays flat and the x term vanishes.

name: curvature
text: Now match the bend. Cosine's second derivative at zero is minus one. Subtracting one-half x squared bends our line into a parabola that shares the exact same curvature.

name: factorial
text: Why divide by two, and then by factorials? Differentiating x to the n pulls down n, then n minus one, all the way to n factorial. Dividing by n factorial cancels that cascade.

name: hug
text: Watch what happens as we add degree four, six, eight, and ten. Each new term locks in the next derivative at zero, making the polynomial hug cosine over a wider and wider interval.

name: formula
text: Keep going forever and you get the Taylor series: the n-th derivative at your anchor point, divided by n factorial, times x minus a to the n.

name: caveat
text: For cosine, this series converges everywhere. Other smooth curves, like one over one plus x squared, only hug inside a fixed radius before shooting off.

name: lesson
text: Still, the core insight holds: knowing every derivative at a single point lets you rebuild a curve far away.
